claims.text: CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy-alloy powder compacts can be produced from mechanically alloyed powders.
The target powder compacts may also be composed of atomized high-entropy-alloy powders.
These high-entropy-alloy powders normally require high sintering temperatures under conventional heating.
Spark plasma sintering can be applied to mechanically alloyed high-entropy-alloy powders.
The proposed SPS cycle uses a heating rate of approximately 50 °C/min and a dwell time of approximately 10 minutes.
SPS can be conducted in a vacuum environment for CoCrFeNiTi powder.
The conventional comparator uses slower heating and longer dwell times than the proposed SPS cycle.
Rapid heating and short hold times produce localized high temperatures at particle contacts.
Pulsed electrical current stimulates diffusion during SPS.
Rapid heating and short hold times limit grain growth.
Enhanced diffusion kinetics reduce the time required for particle bonding and densification.
SPS lowers the temperature required to achieve full densification compared with conventional sintering.
SPS will provide comparable or improved densification at a lower sintering temperature.
SPS will provide a refined microstructure relative to conventional sintering.
The required sintering temperature may be reduced by approximately 100–200 °C.
The method is most effective for electrically conductive powder compacts.
Materials that interact poorly with pulsed current or have substantially different thermal properties may show limited benefit.
The achievable temperature reduction depends on powder characteristics, compaction density, material identity, and SPS equipment.
Density, grain size, porosity, and phase composition can be compared between identical SPS and conventionally sintered powder compacts.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in required sintering temperature while retaining equivalent densification and microstructural quality would falsify the hypothesis.
